nameStory: The curly woodlouse gets its name from its impressive ability to roll up into a tight ball when threatened, curling its segmented body like a tiny armadillo. This defensive behavior makes it look like a small gray pill or marble, which is why some people call them 'roly-polies' or 'pill bugs.'
description: Curly woodlice are small, oval-shaped crustaceans that live on land despite being more closely related to shrimp than insects. They have segmented, armor-like shells that are typically gray to dark gray in color and can roll completely into a ball when disturbed. These little creatures grow to about half an inch long and have seven pairs of legs that help them scurry under logs, rocks, and leaf litter. Unlike insects, they breathe through gills and need moist environments to survive.

idTips.label: Rolling ability
idTips.description: Can roll into a perfect, tight ball when touched - like a tiny gray marble that feels smooth and hard

idTips.label: Body texture
idTips.description: Smooth, shiny segments that feel like hard plastic when gently touched, not rough or bumpy

idTips.label: Color pattern
idTips.description: Uniform gray to dark gray color without distinct markings or mottling

idTips.label: Movement style
idTips.description: Moves with a quick, scuttling motion on seven pairs of legs, then instantly balls up when disturbed

idTips.label: Size and shape
idTips.description: About the size of a large pea when rolled up, oval-shaped when extended with clearly visible body segments

idTips.label: Antennae
idTips.description: Two short antennae that are much smaller than the body length, often hard to see when the animal is moving

habitat: Look for curly woodlice in moist, dark places throughout New England's forests, gardens, and parks. They thrive under rotting logs, beneath stones, in compost piles, and among fallen leaves where the soil stays damp. You'll often find them in suburban gardens under mulch or in basement window wells where moisture collects.

seasonality.spring: Active as soil warms up, often found under garden mulch and emerging from winter hiding spots under logs and stones.
seasonality.summer: Most active during humid evenings and after rain showers. Look under watering areas in gardens and beneath outdoor furniture.
seasonality.fall: Gathering in groups under logs and leaf piles, preparing for winter. Often found when raking leaves or moving garden debris.
seasonality.winter: Hidden deep under logs, stones, or in basements where they remain somewhat active in protected, unfrozen areas.

funFact: Curly woodlice are actually crustaceans that still breathe through gills and must drink water through their rear end - they literally cannot drink through their mouth and will die if their environment becomes too dry for their gills to function!
confusionNotes: Often confused with common pillbugs, but curly woodlice have a smoother, shinier appearance and roll into a more perfect sphere. Memory trick: 'Curly is smooth and shiny like a marble, while common pillbugs look more matte and textured like a dull bead.'
contextualKnowledge: Many people call all rolling woodlice 'pill bugs' or 'roly-polies,' but these names actually refer to several different species. Despite living on land, woodlice are crustaceans (like crabs and lobsters) that evolved from marine ancestors, making them one of the few crustacean groups that successfully colonized terrestrial environments.
compareHints: Since this is the only Cylisticus species commonly found in New England, compare it with other rolling woodlice in the region. Curly woodlice have smoother, shinier shells and form more perfect spheres than most other species. They also tend to be more uniformly gray without the mottled patterns seen in many related species.
